# Discussion

Numerous studies have shown that climate warming, nitrogen deposition, and increased grazing can all lead to plant diversity losses [@klein2004experimental; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @wu2020additive; @shangguan2024plant; @anderson2025experimental; @Austrheim2001-nu; @klein2004experimental; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @post2023large]. We also found the typical negative effects on diversity of nitrogen deposition in this study as well as of warming in the sub-alpine. However, diversity actually increased with warming along most of the nitrogen gradient in the alpine and clipping had only minimal net effects on diversity. The major change diversity occurred at levels of nitrogen addition beyond 10 kg N ha\^-1\^ y^-1^, which is the critical load for significant changes in the structure and function of alpine and sub-alpine grasslands [@bobbink2011review]. In this study, we take a step further by disentangling the direct and indirect effects of these three global change drivers, to understand their underlying mechanisms and to generalise across drivers and climate context. Specifically, we tested whether these global change drivers all operate on diversity indirectly, mediated through community biomass, which reflects the magnitude and type of competition. If that were true, we could predict changes in plant biodiversity through general patterns and trend in community biomass and bypass the need to understand the direct effects of specific global change drivers.

We found only partial support for our hypothesis, with indirect effects through community biomass having substantial effects in the alpine community, but relatively little impact in the sub-alpine community. Warming also had direct effects on diversity in both communities, while direct effects of nitrogen addition were only found in the sub-alpine community. Below, we explore impacts on community biomass, community biomass-mediated effects on diversity in this experiment and the mechanisms underlying the direct effects of each of the global change drivers, including why both direct and indirect mechanisms might differ between the alpine and sub-alpine communities. Finally, we discuss the implications for our ability to generalise impacts of global change drivers.

### Community biomass is more temperature and nitrogen limited in the alpine

A first step in assessing the global change impacts on diversity is quantifying the magnitude of these effect on community biomass. In line with the first part of our hypothesis, we found a strong increase in community biomass with warming and nitrogen addition in both alpine and sub-alpine communities, paralleling the findings of previous studies manipulating one or both of these drivers in alpine grasslands [@elmendorf2012plot; @Humbert2016-wg; @Zhang2023-xg]. Warming can increase biomass because of higher rates of photosynthesis, a longer growing season, or because higher microbial activity can increase nutrient availability, while nitrogen addition directly increases nutrient availability. The magnitude of the biomass response differed however between the two sites. The alpine site was strongly temperature and nutrient limited, resulting in a doubling in community biomass under the combined warming and nitrogen treatment (WxN) compared to the single treatments. In contrast, the sub-additive biomass response to warming and nitrogen addition in the sub-alpine site suggests growth limitation by alternative factors. Given that the sub-alpine site is inherently more productive under unmanipulated conditions (Supplemental Table 2), growth may be constrained by light availability or the co-limitation of other nutrients, such as phosphorus [light ref; @harpole2016addition]. Interestingly, the warmed alpine and ambient sub-alpine communities, which effectively experienced the same climate conditions, showed nearly identical responses to nitrogen addition (similar slope in @fig-1-biomass-diversity a). This suggests that alpine plant communities are not intrinsically less productive than those at lower elevation, but are thermally limited and under warmer conditions they can exhibit a nitrogen limitation equivalent to that of sub-alpine communities.

### Community biomass mediates effects of global change on diversity

There was a negative indirect effect of all three global change drivers mediated through biomass in both communities, although it was only significant in the alpine community (@fig-cut-final-diversity). Nevertheless, species' environmental affinities suggest that community biomass plays an important role even in the sub-alpine community. The net indirect effect of the global change drivers on the diversity indices tended to be negative, except for richness in the sub-alpine community (Supplement Figure S6), suggesting greater local extinction than colonisation and/or increasing dominance in most cases. For both communities, we see a significant shift towards more light-demanding species with increasing community biomass, suggesting greater competition for light [e.g. @olsen2016facilitation]. A similar shift is evident in both communities for the warming and nitrogen addition treatments, which has been observed previously [@Klanderud2005-yx; @Wang2012-cj; @Fu2016-dw]. One possible explanation of the lack of significant biomass-mediated effect on diversity at the sub-alpine community is that the alpine community was more temperature and nutrient limited therefore simply had a bigger change in biomass in response to warming and nitrogen addition (alpine: two times the biomass with WxN; sub-alpine: 1.5 times the biomass with WxN compared to single treatments; Supplement Figure S5). In turn, this would lead to a smaller impact on diversity. A complementary explanation is that the sub-alpine is more productive in unmanipulated conditions (Supplemental Table 2) and therefore may already have intense competition for light. Even with a similar magnitude of biomass response to warming or nitrogen, many light-demanding species may already be absent (consistent with @fig-toenails), leaving less room for further diversity loss. If these arguments are correct, it suggests that less productive communities are likely to see the biggest declines in diversity from global change.

Clipping and grazing effects on the diversity indices were always mediated through community biomass, except for a direct clipping effect on evenness in the sub-alpine community. In line with many other studies, we found that clipping prevented the loss of diversity and evenness under warming and nitrogen levels above 10 kg N ha^-1^ y^-1^ in the alpine community (@fig-1-biomass-diversity b), suggesting this was related to competitive release [@Austrheim2001-nu; @klein2004experimental; @niedrist2009plant; @Bernes2015-yg; @kaarlejarvi2017herbivores; @post2023large]. Interestingly, higher biomass and warming led to a shift to species with higher grazing tolerance in the alpine, but not in the sub-alpine community. In the same experiment, we have shown that warming shifts the alpine community to more resource acquisitive traits [@halbritter2025effects], suggesting a shift towards a community with a higher tolerance for grazing [@lebbink2024plant; @archibald2019unified]. Since the overall grazing effects were similar to the clipping treatments, it suggests that our simulated grazing treatment is comparable to natural grazing and that additional effects of grazing, such as different timing of biomass removal, trampling, and fertilisation from the animals did not override the effect of biomass removal per se.

### Direct effects of global change on diversity

Warming had a direct positive effect on diversity, species richness, and evenness in the alpine community (@fig-cut-final-diversity), which likely reflects a combination of increase in abundance of warm-adapted species and colonisation by species with a higher temperature requirement from the vegetation surrounding the transplanted community. This is supported by a strong shift in the distribution of temperature affinities with warming (@fig-toenails b). In contrast, in the sub-alpine community, warming had a strong negative direct effect on diversity and species richness, but without any accompanying shift in distribution of species' temperature affinity, which were already quite high even in unmanipulated conditions. Instead, the loss of species seems to be related to a loss of drought-tolerant species (i.e. *Carex bigelowii*, *C. pilulifera*, and *Phleum alpinum*). This was somewhat surprising since we expected and found warming to be generally associated with a decline in soil moisture in both sites (Supplement Figures 1 and 2, Supplement Table 1).

Nitrogen addition had a direct negative effect on diversity in both communities, but the effect was much stronger and significant in the sub-alpine community, where evenness, but not richness decreased. This suggests a shift in abundance of species rather than a loss of species. This is unlikely due to a shift in nutrient demanding species since such a shift only occurred in the alpine community and was very small in the sub-alpine community. Species' environmental affinities however suggest that the strong direct effect of nitrogen addition was a consequence of acidification following fertilizing [@Kimmel2020-fo]. In both communities, there was a strong and significant shift towards more acid tolerant species with increasing nitrogen. The acidification could have been stronger in the sub-alpine community, because that community is less nutrient limited, generally, although not always associated with an increase in available calcium at high levels of nitrogen addition, which can be released from the bedrock under acid conditions.

Consistent with the minimal net effects of clipping on diversity (@fig-1-biomass-diversity b), we found no direct effect of clipping or grazing on diversity, except that clipping decreased evenness directly in the sub-alpine community. Further, the measured environmental affinities of the species showed no significant shifts in response to clipping. In the alpine site, species loss was reduced at both clipping intensities, though only the intensive treatment significantly increased diversity. This suggests that the medium clipping intensity was insufficient to reduce light competition effectively, also shown by less reduction in biomass (@fig-1-biomass-diversity a). Similarly, at the sub-alpine site, none of the clipping treatments prevented species loss, despite a significant reduction in community biomass. Such site-specific responses align with previous findings that grazing effects on plant diversity can vary along elevational gradients [@Speed2013-to]. <!--  Problem: we did see some effect of biomass on light affinities -->

Our study was conducted over three years and thus looks at short-term responses, which can differ from long-term responses [(*56*, *57*)](https://paperpile.com/c/KKq9O1/egX7+3xXg). Long-term experiments across different climatic contexts are needed to understand where and how local adaptation of grazing regimes can be used as a tool to mitigate impacts of warming and pollution and inform adaptive management strategies that benefit biodiversity.

### Conclusions and implications

Our findings show that community biomass can be used as a general indicator of mechanisms mediating global change impacts on plant diversity, but this was stronger in colder and unproductive alpine grassland. While several of these drivers including warming, nitrogen addition, clipping, and grazing operate through this shared pathway, these indirect effects do not always dominate. Warming and nitrogen addition operated via multiple mechanisms, and specifically in more productive ecosystems, where other factors limited community biomass, direct effects can override these biomass-mediated effects. We advocate for coordinated distributed experiments across broad environmental gradients [@fraser2013coordinated; @prager2022integrating] and the synthesis of existing experiment across different ecosystems to generalize this predictive framework and understand under which conditions the direct effects are important. Finally, our application of Ellenberg values to characterize environmental affinities is a useful approach to disentangle the underlying shifts species response to global change.
